feat: add `byte_start`/`byte_end` positions to `Token` and `Tag` (#143)

* feat: add `byte_start`/`byte_end` positions to `Token` and `Tag`, change `cut*` to return `Vec<Token>`

Breaking changes:
- `Token` struct: added `byte_start`, `byte_end` fields
- `Tag` struct: added `start`, `end`, `byte_start`, `byte_end` fields
- `cut()`, `cut_all()`, `cut_for_search()` now return `Vec<Token>` instead of `Vec<&str>`
- `tokenize()` now delegates to `cut()`/`cut_for_search()` directly

Performance:
- Precompute byte-to-unicode lookup table only for `cut_all` (overlapping tokens)
- Use zero-allocation incremental unicode tracking for `cut`/`cut_for_search`
- Added `make_token_incremental()` using UTF-8 leading byte counting
- `debug_assert` guards for subslice validity and char boundary correctness

* Use expect-test for snapshot testing

* Eliminate `byte_to_unicode_table` allocation in `cut_all` path

Split `cut_all` into dedicated `cut_all_toplevel`/`cut_all_tokens` that
compute unicode positions inline via `char_indices().enumerate()` and
leading-byte counting, avoiding the `vec![0usize; s.len() + 1]` allocation
that was the main source of `_platform_memset` overhead.

Also removes `cut_all` branch checks from the `cut`/`cut_for_search` hot
path, improving `no_hmm` by ~9%.

Replace regex splitting with hand-rolled `SplitByCharacterClass` (#144)

Replace `RE_HAN_DEFAULT`, `RE_HAN_CUT_ALL`, `RE_SKIP_CUT_ALL`, and
`RE_SKIP_DEFAULT` regexes in `lib.rs` with inline character classifiers
(`is_han_default`, `is_han_cut_all`, `is_skip_cut_all`) and a generic
`SplitByCharacterClass` iterator.

Also replace HMM `RE_HAN` with `is_hmm_han` classifier, keeping only
`RE_SKIP` as regex due to its complex pattern `([a-zA-Z0-9]+(?:.\d+)?%?)`.

Profiling showed regex `find_fwd`/`find_rev` accounted for ~29% of CPU
time; this drops to <1% with the character class approach.

Benchmark improvements (vs previous commit on `add-byte-positions`):
- `no_hmm`:         1.22 µs → 1.02 µs (-16%)
- `with_hmm`:       1.82 µs → 1.50 µs (-18%)
- `cut_for_search`: 2.31 µs → 2.00 µs (-14%)

Optimize HMM emit prob lookups and precompute log frequencies (#145)

- Change HMM emit probability maps from phf::Map<&str, f64> to
  phf::Map<char, f64> since all keys are single characters. This
  avoids string hashing/comparison overhead in the Viterbi inner loop.

- Precompute log(freq) in Record::log_freq to eliminate per-lookup
  f64::ln() calls in calc().

- Simplify viterbi() to iterate chars directly instead of using
  byte offset peekable iterator.

- Use direct array indexing for TRANS_PROBS instead of .get().unwrap().

Benchmarks show 9-13% improvement on segmentation workloads.

feat: add posseg (part-of-speech tagging) HMM for OOV words (#146)

Implement a compound-state HMM Viterbi (4 positions × 64 POS tags = 256
states) for POS-tagging unknown/OOV Chinese words, ported from Python
jieba's posseg module.

- Add `posseg.rs` with dense 256×256 transition matrix for O(1) lookup
- Embed probability data (start, trans, emit, char_state_tab) via
  `include_flate`, gated on `default-dict` feature
- Improve `tag()` to use posseg HMM for OOV CJK words instead of falling
  back to `"x"` (e.g. `"张尧"` now correctly tagged as `"nr"`/person name)
- Add conversion script (`scripts/convert_posseg.py`) for regenerating
  `posseg.txt` from Python jieba's pickle files
- Add benchmark for `tag_with_oov` (~2.5µs per call)

Add tag field to Keyword struct

Closes #86. The extract_tags API now includes POS tag information
on each Keyword, matching the Python jieba API.

Optimize jieba hot paths (#152)

* Merge HMM emission probability lookups

Generate one phf::Map<char, [f64; 4]> for builtin HMM emission probabilities and store runtime HmmModel emissions as char -> [f64; 4]. Viterbi now does one emission lookup per input character instead of one lookup per state per character, and runtime models avoid UTF-8 re-encoding on lookup.

Measured with: cargo build --release -p weicheng && hyperfine --warmup 3 --runs 10 './target/release/weicheng'. Result: 732.8ms mean baseline -> 663.5ms mean after this change, a 9.5% improvement. Verification: cargo test -p jieba-rs --all-features passed.

* Cache dictionary log total

Store log_total on Jieba and refresh it whenever total changes through load_dict, add_word, or clear. calc and suggest_freq now reuse the cached logarithm instead of recomputing (total as f64).ln() for each block.

Measured with the ./target/release/weicheng internal timer over 10 runs after the HMM emission commit. Result: median 565ms -> 562ms, a 0.5% improvement. Verification: cargo test -p jieba-rs --all-features passed.

* Reuse DAG storage for cut_all

Hoist the StaticSparseDAG allocation out of cut_all_tokens and keep one reusable DAG in cut_all_toplevel, clearing it after each matched block. This avoids allocating fresh sparse DAG storage for every CJK block in cut_all.

Measured with: cargo bench -p jieba-rs --features tfidf,textrank -- cut/cut_all. Result: 722.05ns baseline -> 633.44ns after this change, a 12.5% improvement. Verification: cargo test -p jieba-rs --all-features passed.

* Use explicit max loop in route calculation

Replace the iterator map/max_by chain in calc with a direct loop that tracks the best probability and preserves the existing tie-break toward the larger byte_end. This avoids iterator adapter overhead in the route dynamic-programming hot path.

Measured with: cargo bench -p jieba-rs --features tfidf,textrank -- cut/. Results: cut/no_hmm 646.83ns -> 592.07ns (8.2% faster), cut/with_hmm 868.17ns -> 778.18ns (10.4% faster), and cut/cut_for_search 1.0472us -> 983.70ns (6.1% faster). Verification: cargo test -p jieba-rs --all-features passed.

* Precompute TextRank keyword candidates

Build a candidate_ids table once per TextRank extraction, mapping each tag position to its eligible word id. The co-occurrence loop now uses two array reads per pair instead of repeatedly checking allowed POS, allocating in is_keyword, and looking up word ids inside the span loop.

Measured with: cargo bench -p jieba-rs --features tfidf,textrank -- keywords/textrank. Result: 4.7337us baseline -> 3.6723us after this change, a 22.1% improvement. Verification: cargo test -p jieba-rs --all-features passed.

* Use hash lookup for keyword stop words

Keep the public stop_words BTreeSet API, but build an internal FxHashSet lookup table in KeywordExtractConfig. Keyword filtering now uses the hash table for stop-word membership while preserving the existing builder and accessor types.

Measured with: cargo bench -p jieba-rs --features tfidf,textrank -- keywords/. Results: keywords/tfidf 2.0706us -> 1.7540us (15.3% faster) and keywords/textrank 3.6809us -> 3.3084us (10.1% faster). Verification: cargo test -p jieba-rs --all-features passed.

* Avoid unnecessary keyword lowercasing

Scan each candidate keyword once to count characters and detect uppercase characters, check the stop-word table directly, and only allocate a lowercase string when uppercase text needs case-folded lookup. This removes the unconditional to_lowercase allocation from keyword filtering.

Measured with: cargo bench -p jieba-rs --features tfidf,textrank -- keywords/. Results: keywords/tfidf 1.7540us -> 1.4881us (15.2% faster) and keywords/textrank 3.3084us -> 3.0799us (6.9% faster). Verification: cargo test -p jieba-rs --all-features passed.

* Skip duplicate checks for initial default dict load

Route load_default_dict through a private unique-dictionary loader when the Jieba instance is empty. The bundled default dictionary has unique word keys, so initial construction can avoid an exact_match_search before every cedar update while public load_dict and non-empty load_default_dict calls keep the duplicate/update semantics.

Measured with: cargo bench -p jieba-rs --features tfidf,textrank -- jieba/new. Result: 55.691ms baseline -> 51.341ms after this change, a 7.8% improvement. Verification: cargo test -p jieba-rs --all-features passed.

* Apply clippy cleanups in tag helpers

Address clippy suggestions in POS tagging helpers after dropping the posseg scratch-buffer optimization. This keeps the validation command warning-free without changing the public API or claiming a performance optimization.

fix: escape the dot in RE_SKIP to match upstream jieba (#158)

RE_SKIP left the dot unescaped, so it matched any character instead of a
literal dot. The ASCII path never reaches the Viterbi decoder, so this
expression alone decides how alphanumeric runs are cut, and jieba-rs absorbed
one arbitrary character into a token whenever digits followed it:

    WES-5.4.5     ["WES-5", ".", "4.5"]      -> ["WES", "-", "5.4", ".", "5"]
    G260911-0711  ["G260911-0711"]           -> ["G260911", "-", "0711"]

The new behaviour matches upstream jieba (jieba/finalseg/__init__.py:78).
Decimals and percentages, which the expression exists for, are unaffected.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

perf: hand-roll the RE_SKIP scan and drop the regex dependency (#160)

hmm.rs was the only remaining user of `regex`, for a pattern simple enough to
scan directly: `([a-zA-Z0-9]+(?:\.\d+)?%?)`. Replacing it removes `regex`, and
with it regex-automata, regex-syntax and aho-corasick, from the dependency
graph.

Every character the pattern can match is ASCII, so the block is walked as
bytes; a UTF-8 continuation byte is never alphanumeric, so every boundary the
scan produces falls on a character boundary.

Output is byte-identical to the regex version over 5,398 inputs across cut,
cut_for_search, cut_all and tag. Benchmarks that reach the skip path are 9-11%
faster.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix: keep connected alphanumeric runs together in cut (#162)

`re_skip` exists so that non-Chinese text passes through without being
segmented, but its expression could carry at most one separator and required
digits after it. Text it failed to recognise was not passed through — it was
fragmented, and which identifiers survived depended on the character class of
whatever followed the separator:

    G260911-0711  ->  G260911-0711     a digit follows the hyphen
    ISU-CNS24093  ->  ISU | - | CNS24093   a letter does
    1.2.3         ->  1.2 | . | 3      the second dot ends the match

`cut` now keeps an alphanumeric run joined by `.`, `_` or `-` together, with
the separator repeatable and either side letters or digits. A trailing
separator is not part of the token, and decimals and percentages -- what the
expression was originally for -- are unaffected.

Search mode offers the parts as well, as it already does for Chinese compounds,
so nothing becomes unfindable: `ISU-CNS24093` is still reachable by `ISU` and
by `CNS24093`. Parts are only offered when they could be searched on their own,
so a purely numeric fragment of a version number and a single character are
left out.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Bump version to 0.10.4

perf: optimize tagging, dictionary loading, HMM lookups and per-call allocations (#163)

* perf: resolve posseg candidate states and emissions in one lookup

The OOV tagger did one hash lookup per character for its candidate
states and then one more per candidate state for the emission
probability, across 256 separate maps. Store each character's candidate
states with their emissions inline and sorted by state, so a character
costs one lookup and its position groups are contiguous ranges.

The transition table only contains position-legal pairs (B after E/S,
M and E after B/M, S after E/S), so restricting each state's
predecessors to those groups is exact and halves the inner loop.
Characters that have emissions but no explicit state list keep only
the states that have an emission: a state whose emission is MIN_FLOAT
sums to exactly MIN_FLOAT and can never be selected.

Viterbi scratch buffers now live in a thread-local, and guess_tag
consumes spans as they are decoded instead of building a Vec.

Measured with cargo bench -p jieba-rs --features tfidf,textrank:
jieba/tag_with_oov 2.23 µs -> 1.47 µs (-34%). Tagging the weicheng
text 20 times: 486 ms -> 383 ms. Output is byte-identical over the
whole text for cut, cut_all, cut_for_search and tag.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* perf: parse the embedded dictionary in place and intern tags

Loading the default dictionary went through BufReader::read_line,
which copies every line and re-validates it as UTF-8, and then
split_whitespace. The embedded file is a well-formed `word freq tag`
list, so parse it straight from the string with split_ascii_whitespace,
and reserve the record vectors up front from a line count.

Every record also owned a Box<str> for its tag, one heap allocation
per word for a few dozen distinct values. Tags are now interned into a
table and records store an index. The log frequencies move into their
own dense Vec<f64>, so the route calculation reads an 8-byte array
instead of 32-byte records.

Measured: jieba/new 53.6 ms -> 41.5 ms (-22%). Cut benchmarks are
unchanged within noise on the short sentence.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* perf: index HMM emissions by character and unroll Viterbi

The builtin HMM looked emissions up in a phf map, which hashes the
character with SipHash on every step. The segmenter only runs the HMM
over [一-鿕] blocks, so the macro now emits a u16 index over
that range plus a table of emission rows: a lookup is two dependent
loads. The one emission key outside the range can never be looked up
and is dropped. This removes phf and phf_codegen from the dependency
graph.

The Viterbi step replaces the iterator/max_by chains over the two
allowed predecessors with explicit comparisons, keeping the same
last-wins tie behaviour.

Measured: cut/with_hmm 776 ns -> 729 ns (-6%), cut/cut_for_search -4%,
jieba/tag -4.6%. Cutting the weicheng text 30 times: 312 ms -> 299 ms.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* perf: reuse segmentation scratch per thread and stream words to tokens

Every cut allocated a route, a DAG, a word vector and a token vector,
and borrowed the HMM context from a thread-local once per block. The
route, DAG and HMM context now share one thread-local scratch that is
borrowed once per call, released again only if a very large input grew
it. Words go straight from the DAG walk into the token vector through a
sink closure, so the intermediate Vec<&str> and its second pass are
gone.

The DAG drops its touched-offset bookkeeping and iterator size hint:
positions are opened in increasing order, so the offset table only
grows at the end and clearing it is a truncate. The route no longer
needs clearing between blocks, since every entry read is either written
first or is the sentinel at the block end. Single-character tests use
the leading byte's UTF-8 width instead of decoding two characters.

Measured against the previous commit: cut/no_hmm 628 ns -> 577 ns,
cut/with_hmm 729 ns -> 708 ns, cut/cut_for_search 960 ns -> 931 ns.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* perf: index the DAG by character and carry word ids through the route

The DAG offset table was indexed by byte, which meant filling the gaps
for continuation bytes on every start. Both readers walk characters in
order anyway, so index it by character and make start() a plain push.

The route now records the id of the word each step chose. tag() uses it
directly for dictionary words instead of repeating the exact-match
search for every token, and only looks up what the segmentation did
not: HMM output, joined ASCII runs and non-CJK characters. cut, tag and
cut_for_search all consume a shared cut_each core, so cut_for_search and
tag no longer materialise an intermediate token vector.

Measured against the previous commit: cut/no_hmm 577 ns -> 530 ns,
cut/with_hmm 708 ns -> 643 ns, cut/cut_for_search 931 ns -> 786 ns,
jieba/tag 858 ns -> 738 ns. Whole-text search 227 ms -> 199 ms, tag
368 ms -> 351 ms.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* perf: scalar CJK fast path, live-state posseg Viterbi, merged keyword maps

is_cjk matched nine ranges in one expression, which LLVM vectorised
into a NEON compare-and-reduce sequence per character; it was ~9% of
cut. Test the main block [一-鿿] on its own first and reach the
extension ranges only for other non-ASCII characters.

The posseg Viterbi step scanned the transition matrix column-wise with
a 2 KB stride and re-checked unreachable predecessors for every
candidate. Store the matrix transposed so predecessors of one state are
a row, and carry only the reachable states of the previous step, with
their scores, in a compact list grouped by position.

The keyword extractors kept two hash maps keyed by the same words (term
frequency and tag, or id and tag); each is now one map.

Measured against the previous commit: jieba/tag_with_oov 1.43 µs ->
0.95 µs, keywords/tfidf 1.40 µs -> 1.37 µs. Whole-text tag 334 ms ->
297 ms with interleaved min-of-5 runs.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* perf: insert the sorted default dictionary in reverse order

cedar keeps each node's children ordered. A child whose label is larger
than its siblings' is appended after walking the whole sibling chain;
one whose label is smaller goes in first. The embedded dictionary is
sorted, so inserting it front to back always took the slow path.
Iterating the lines in reverse makes every insertion the O(1) case.

Word ids change order, which nothing observes: the trie is the same
set of words, and output over the weicheng text is byte-identical.
Cut throughput is unchanged within noise across six interleaved runs.

Measured: jieba/new 41.5 ms -> 38.9 ms (-6%).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* bench: measure multithreaded throughput over a whole text

The multithreaded group cut one short sentence 1000 times, about
650 µs of work split across every rayon worker. Each iteration was
dominated by fork-join setup, worker wake-up and work stealing, and
identical runs swung by 30-100%, so the number could not tell faster
code from slower.

Both variants now segment every line of the weicheng text, with
with_min_len(4) to keep splits coarse, and report throughput in bytes
of that text. An iteration is several milliseconds of segmentation, and
confidence intervals are within about 1%. CodSpeed history for these
two benchmarks starts over.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* perf: replace cedarwood with a character-level hash trie

cedarwood is a byte-level double-array trie. Walking a CJK word costs
three dependent transitions per character, each with a further load to
test for a word ending there, two thirds of which land on UTF-8
continuation bytes where a word can never end. Building it inserts
349k keys one at a time into a structure that relocates blocks as it
grows; it was over half of Jieba::new.

The replacement is built for the segmenter's one access pattern: from
every character of the input, enumerate the dictionary words that
start there. The root's transitions for BMP characters are a directly
indexed table, so the first step is a cache-resident array load. Every
other transition is one entry in an open-addressing hash table keyed
by (parent node, char), and the entry carries the child's id, whether
it has children, and the id of the word ending there, so a walk needs
one probe per character and no separate word-boundary lookup. Inserts
are O(1) per character, so dictionary loading no longer depends on key
order and the reverse-order insertion goes away.

A position's walk is a chain of dependent loads that the processor
cannot overlap with the next position's, so the walk touches the slot
that the second character of the position three steps ahead will need;
by the time the walk gets there it is in cache. This costs one
cache-resident root lookup per position and is what turns the
structure's fewer loads into time saved. Level-synchronous walking
(all positions one character at a time) and an explicit prefetch
instruction were both measured and were not better.

The default dictionary has 498k trie nodes for 349k words; the table
holds them in 2^20 16-byte slots plus a 512 KiB root table, less than
cedar's arrays, and RSS after Jieba::new drops from 76 MB to 68 MB.
Output is byte-identical over the weicheng text for cut, cut_all,
cut_for_search and tag, with and without HMM.

Measured, whole text, interleaved min of 4 runs, cedar -> trie:
Jieba::new x5 186 ms -> 97 ms; cut with HMM x30 264 -> 243 ms; cut
without HMM 224 -> 197 ms; cut_all 152 -> 135 ms; cut_for_search 195 ->
189 ms; tag 299 -> 299 ms. Criterion against the previous commit:
jieba/new -46%, cut/no_hmm -8%, jieba/tag -6%, multithreaded
single_thread -5.6% and multi_thread -5.1%; the short single-sentence
HMM and search entries are flat because one repeated sentence keeps
cedar's nodes cache-hot.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* perf: filter trie children before probing

On the weicheng text a level-3 probe happens at 31% of positions, but
only 5% of positions have a three-character dictionary prefix: a
quarter of all positions paid a random cache miss to learn that a
2-character node has children, just not this one. Fan-out below the
root is tiny (median 1, p90 3), so a small per-node filter of the
characters its children start with rejects most of those probes.

Each slot has 19 unused key bits and 8 unused child-pointer bits. The
key's high 16 bits and the pointer's high 8 bits now hold two
Bloom-style bit sets over the node's children, set when a child is
inserted and tested before every probe; a node has children iff a bit
is set, which replaces the has-children flag. Probes compare keys
under a mask. Node ids are limited to 2^24, which is 34 times the
default dictionary's node count.

Measured, whole text, interleaved min of 4: cut without HMM 200 ->
184 ms, cut with HMM 246 -> 230 ms, cut_all 133 -> 126 ms,
cut_for_search 189 -> 176 ms, tag 280 -> 267 ms; Jieba::new x5 96 ->
99 ms. Output is byte-identical.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* perf: decode each block once and index the route by character

A block was decoded four times: by the splitter to find its bounds, by
the trie walk to collect its characters, by calc walking char_indices
backwards, and by every token to count its characters. The splitter
now records each character of the run it yields, as (byte offset,
char), into a per-thread buffer, and every later pass works from that.

With characters in hand, the DAG, the route and the token builder use
character indices instead of byte offsets: a DAG edge ends at a
character index, the route has one entry per character rather than per
byte (a third as many for CJK), calc iterates the index range
backwards, and a token's character count is the difference of two
indices, so nothing counts UTF-8 lead bytes any more except words the
HMM produces. Byte offsets come back from the buffer when a word is
sliced.

Measured, whole text, interleaved min of 4: cut without HMM 182 ->
158 ms, cut with HMM 229 -> 206 ms, cut_all 125 -> 105 ms,
cut_for_search 175 -> 163 ms, tag 264 -> 249 ms. Output is
byte-identical.

* perf: iterate DAG edge lists as slices

Edge lists sit back to back in one array, each followed by its
sentinel, so a character's list is the slice from its start to just
before the next list's start. Handing calc and cut_all that slice
replaces the cursor iterator that re-checked bounds and the sentinel on
every edge.

Measured, whole text, interleaved min of 4: cut without HMM 160 ->
157 ms, cut with HMM 204 -> 202 ms, cut_for_search 160 -> 157 ms.
Output is byte-identical.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: break HMM Viterbi ties the way the original comparison did

The unrolled Viterbi let the later of the two predecessor candidates win an
equal score, but the comparison it replaced ordered `(score, State)` pairs,
so a tie went to the state with the larger index. Two rows of
`ALLOWED_PREV_STATUS` listed the larger state first, which flipped the
choice for `Middle` and `Single` and changed the segmentation of runs of
characters without emission data: `龘龘龘` came out as `龘龘 | 龘` instead
of three single characters.

List every row in ascending state order so the second candidate is the one
the original tie-break chose, and add a regression test.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: release the per-thread character buffer after a huge input

`release_if_huge` dropped an oversized route and DAG but not the character
buffer the splitter fills, so a thread that once segmented a very long
block kept that allocation for as long as it lived. Cap every scratch
buffer by bytes rather than entries, which also brings the route's limit
down from 24 MiB to 4 MiB, and apply the cap to the characters too.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: bound the initial capacity of result vectors

`cut_for_search` and `tag` used to size their result from the token count
of a completed `cut`; streaming the tokens replaced that with the same
half-the-byte-length guess `cut` makes. For a long input with few tokens,
such as a run of ASCII letters, the returned vector then carried megabytes
of unused capacity. Reserve at most 4096 entries up front and let the
vector grow for longer inputs; a short sentence still allocates once.

* Bump version to 0.11.0

`jieba-rs` now reads the emission table as the dense `EMIT_INDEX` and
`EMIT_PROBS` arrays that `jieba-macros` generates, which no published

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* perf: answer search mode's n-gram lookups from the block's DAG

`cut_for_search` looked every 2- and 3-character substring of each token
up in the trie, after walking the token's characters again for their
byte offsets. The dictionary matches of the block the token came from
already say which of those substrings are words, and the block's decoded
characters give the offsets, so the token sink now carries the token's
position in its block along with the block's DAG and characters, and
search mode reads both instead of repeating the work. `cut` and `tag`
ignore the extra argument.

Whole text, search mode ×20: 152 → 148 ms; criterion `cut/cut_for_search`
-7.7%; `cut/no_hmm` and `cut/with_hmm` unchanged. Output is byte-identical
over the golden set.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: release POS tagging and HMM scratch after a huge input

Tagging keeps its Viterbi buffers in a thread-local of its own, and the
backpointer table is 256 entries per character, so one huge unknown word
pinned tens of megabytes for the life of the thread: tagging 100,000
characters outside the emission table left 63 MiB behind. Cap those
buffers, and the HMM segmenter's, at 4 MiB each like the segmentation
scratch.

The compound HMM also now stops as soon as no state is reachable, before
sizing the backpointer table; the search could only have ended with
nothing to trace back and the same fallback tag for the whole span. For
that 100,000-character word tagging drops from 23 ms to 1.2 ms and the
memory left behind from 63 MiB to 5.6 MiB, all of it buffers under the
cap.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* perf: stop search mode's edge scan at the wanted end

Checking whether a token's 2- or 3-gram is a word scanned every edge at
the position, and with a dictionary of long words that meant running
through all the longer matches for each miss: with words of 4 to 256
`a`s and an 8,192-character input, search mode had become 12% slower
than looking the grams up in the trie. Edges are ordered by end, so the
scan stops at the first one reaching the wanted end. That scenario is now
10% faster than the trie lookups (428 → 383 ms for 40 calls) and
ordinary text is unchanged.

* refactor: consolidate the segmentation helpers after review

Cleanups from a reuse, simplification, efficiency and altitude pass over
the branch, each kept only where an interleaved benchmark against the
previous commit showed no cost:

- One `release_if_huge` helper with a per-buffer budget replaces the
  three copies in the segmentation, HMM and POS scratch; the DAG keeps
  its larger allowance, since regrowing a big edge table costs more than
  holding it.
- `StaticSparseDAG::word_at` answers "is this span a dictionary word"
  from the block's edges, and now serves search mode, `tag` (which no
  longer walks the trie for words the segmentation did not look up) and
  the HMM's check of an unjoined run.
- The two route walkers become one `cut_route<const HMM>` with the same
  inlining shape as before; `RouteEntry` is a named struct.
- `cut_all` absorbs its "toplevel" helper and walks the recorded
  characters instead of re-splitting the block; `load_dict` absorbs its
  inner function; the main CJK range check is one helper.
- POS tagging grows its backpointer table without clearing it (only
  entries this call wrote are read), shares its scratch prologue between
  `guess_tag` and the test helper, and the trie's exact lookup uses a
  `step` helper (the walk keeps its written-out transition: routing it
  through the helper measured slower).
- The HMM's character range is emitted by `jieba-macros` alongside the
  emission table it bounds, so the two cannot drift.

Tried and reverted, because the benchmark binary showed 3-15% on
`cut_for_search` depending on inlining decisions even when the harness
did not: hoisting the DAG build out of the walkers with a span struct as
the word sink, and a `Block` type bundling text and characters.

perf: data-structure and startup optimizations from the performance audit (#164)

* perf: select the IDF median in linear time and parse the embedded table in place

Loading an IDF dictionary pushed every value into a binary heap and then
popped half of them one by one to reach the median, and collected the
fields of every line into a fresh Vec. The values now go into a plain
Vec and the lower median comes from select_nth_unstable, which is
linear; fields are read straight off the split iterator.

The bundled table was also read through BufReader::read_line, which
copies each line and re-validates it as UTF-8. Like the default
dictionary, it is a well-formed in-memory string, so TfIdf::default now
walks its lines directly and reserves the map from a line count.
load_dict keeps its BufRead contract and shares the per-line and median
code.

The median is still that of the values read by one load, duplicates
included, and the lower one for an even count, so results are
unchanged: keyword output is byte-identical over the golden set.

Measured, TfIdf::default, min of 3 interleaved runs: 35.6 ms -> 16.3 ms.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* perf: roll the HMM Viterbi scores instead of keeping the whole table

The recurrence only reads the previous character's four scores, but the
segmentation HMM kept a 4×n score table and read the final scores back
out of it. The scores now roll through two [f64; 4] arrays; only the
predecessor choices are stored, and they are plain states rather than
Options, since the traceback runs a fixed number of steps and the first
row was never read.

Addition order, the higher-state tie choice and the terminal End/Single
choice are unchanged, and runtime models go through the same code.
Output is byte-identical over the golden set.

Measured, whole text, min of 3 interleaved runs: every line through the
HMM (empty dictionary) 14.6 -> 13.3 ms; cut with HMM 65.1 -> 64.1 ms,
search 75.5 -> 74.1 ms, tag 112.4 -> 110.0 ms. Packing the four
predecessor choices into one byte per character on top of this was
measured and made no difference.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* perf: drop the sentinel words from the DAG edge lists

Each character's edge list ended in a 0 word, but the readers already
take a list's bounds from the offset table, so the sentinels were
written and skipped for nothing, and the edge encoding carried a +1 so
that 0 could not be a real edge. The edge array is now plain compressed
sparse row storage: one offset per character plus one past the end,
and a list is the slice between two neighbouring offsets. Ends are
stored as they are.

Output is byte-identical over the golden set.

Measured, whole text, min of 4 interleaved runs: cut without HMM
53.5 -> 52.1 ms, cut_all 50.5 -> 50.0 ms, search 75.3 -> 73.8 ms.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* perf: emit cut_all tokens straight from the trie walk

cut_all built the block's DAG and then enumerated it once, position by
position. The trie walk already visits the words in that order and
nothing else reads the matches of a cut_all block, so the tokens now
come out of the walk's callback and the DAG is not built at all.

Output is byte-identical over the golden set.

Measured, whole text, min of 4 interleaved runs: cut_all 49.6 -> 39.5 ms.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* perf: store the TextRank graph flat and precompute each edge's share

Every one of the 20 ranking sweeps divided each edge's weight by the
destination's total outgoing weight again, and walked a Vec of Vecs
that cost one allocation per vertex. The graph is now compressed sparse
row storage built with one counting sort: per-vertex offsets, a
destination array and, in place of the weight, the quotient it was
divided into, computed once. The sweep is then a dot product over two
contiguous slices.

Neighbour order, self-loops, duplicate edges and the in-place update
order are as before, and the sum is over the same products in the same
order, so ranks are bit-identical: output is byte-identical over the
golden set, including 20- and 500-keyword extractions from 400-line
documents.

Measured, min of 3 interleaved runs: TextRank over every line of the
text 45.5 -> 41.5 ms, a 40-line document x20 19.5 -> 16.7 ms, a 400-line
document x5 76.1 -> 72.0 ms.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* perf: trim the keyword extractors' selection passes

- The allowed-POS list is a few tags at most; membership is a scan of
  the Vec instead of building a BTreeSet<String> per call.
- Both top-k heaps compare a candidate against the current worst and
  replace the root through peek_mut only when it wins, instead of
  pushing every candidate and popping one back out.
- TextRank found the candidate ids in one pass over the tags and then
  did a second pass with another filter and hash lookup per token; the
  ids come out of the first pass now. Rejected tokens keep their
  positions, so the co-occurrence window is unchanged.
- Results are collected while the heap has entries and sized from it,
  instead of looping to top_k, and k = 0 returns early.

The heap comparator is unchanged, so ties resolve as before: output is
byte-identical over the golden set for k = 0, 1, 3, 20 and 500 with and
without an allowed-POS list.

Measured, min of 3 interleaved runs: TextRank over every line
41.8 -> 39.4 ms, 40-line document x20 16.2 -> 14.9 ms, 400-line x5
72.1 -> 65.7 ms; TF-IDF 40-line x20 10.3 -> 9.5 ms, 400-line x5
48.9 -> 45.8 ms.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* perf: index the POS model's character rows directly

The compound HMM looked each character's candidate states up in a hash
map of separately boxed lists. All of the model's characters are in the
BMP, so the lookup is now a load from a 64K-entry u16 table that names
the character's row (0 for a character the model has never seen), with
a small map only for characters beyond the BMP. The rows themselves sit
back to back in one pool, so the model is a few arrays instead of one
allocation per character.

State order, position bounds and the fallback for unseen characters are
unchanged: tags are byte-identical over the golden set.

Measured, whole text, min of 3 interleaved runs: tagging with an empty
dictionary (every word through the compound HMM) 115.1 -> 108.6 ms,
tagging with the default dictionary 107.3 -> 105.2 ms.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* perf: keep POS states and their emissions in separate pools

A row entry was a (u16, f64) pair, 16 bytes with padding, of which the
Viterbi step reads both halves. Storing the states and the emissions in
two parallel arrays makes it 10 bytes per candidate, so a row spans
fewer cache lines. Tags are byte-identical over the golden set.

Measured, whole text, min of 3 interleaved runs: tagging with an empty
dictionary 110.6 -> 108.2 ms; tagging with the default dictionary
unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* perf: embed the data files with zstd instead of deflate

The dictionary, IDF table and POS model are inflated on first use, and

Output is byte-identical over the golden set. A release binary with all

OOV word 18.7 -> 10.8 ms. Warm construction is unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Both extractors called tag() and then walked the returned Vec<Tag>
once. tag() now streams through a crate-private tag_each, and the
extractors count term frequencies or collect candidate ids in its
callback, so the 64-byte Tag list of the whole document is never

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* perf: cut HMM runs from the block's decoded characters

An unjoined run handed to the HMM was decoded twice more: once by the
splitter that finds the runs the model covers, and once by Viterbi
collecting char_indices into its own buffer. The segmenter already has
the block's characters with their byte offsets, so the HMM now takes
that slice: the covered runs are found by classifying the decoded
characters, Viterbi reads them directly, and words are sliced out of
the block by the recorded offsets. The HMM context no longer keeps a
character buffer.

Runs are the same, cut at the same offsets, and the trailing
non-covered text is split as before: output is byte-identical over the
golden set, including mixed ASCII/CJK and supplementary-plane input.

fix: free C API results with the layout they were allocated with (#165)

The result arrays handed to C were leaked from a Vec and freed with
Vec::from_raw_parts(ptr, len, len), but the allocation's capacity was
usually larger: collect() reuses the source allocation when it can, so
the 24 tokens of the benchmark sentence came back with capacity 120
words, 72 tokens or 80 tags. Freeing with a smaller layout than was
allocated is undefined behaviour, even where the system allocator
happens to tolerate it. FfiStr had the same problem: shrink_to_fit does
not promise an exact capacity, yet free rebuilt the String with
capacity = len.

Results are now handed over as boxed slices and strings as boxed str,
which are exactly len elements by construction, so the pointer and
length the C structs keep are enough to free them.

The keyword extractors also took ownership of the caller's allowed-POS
strings through CString::from_raw and freed them with Rust's allocator.
They are read through CStr now and stay the caller's; the parameter is
*const *const c_char accordingly.

The capi tests run on an allocator that records the size of every live
allocation and aborts on a free with a different size; with the old
code the new result/free round-trip tests abort, with this change all
seven pass.

Co-authored-by: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
